vignette:
Dr. Samir Khan presents as a man holding himself together with tremendous, exhausting effort. He sits in the chair opposite me the way he must sit in his own office with patients: composed, thoughtful, his posture a study in professional calm. But his hands, resting on his knees, are clenched so tightly the knuckles are white, a stark contrast to his measured tone.

The story begins fifteen years ago in Lahore. He was twenty-two, a graduate student in psychology, meeting a friend for tea at a small, bustling cafe. He remembers the details with a photographer's clarity: the sticky sweetness of the jalebi they were sharing, the clatter of dishes, the warm afternoon sun slanting through the window. He was explaining a passage from Freud when the world dissolved into a concussive roar. He doesn't remember the sound as much as the feeling of it-a physical force that lifted him and threw him against a wall.

When he came to, the world was silent and white with dust. The air was thick with a smell he would later identify as cordite and burnt sugar, a scent that can still, without warning, ambush him in a grocery store or on the street, bringing him to a dead stop. He was uninjured, miraculously. A few cuts, a ringing in his ears. His friend was not so lucky. Samir doesn't speak about what he saw when the dust began to settle, but his gaze drifts to a point on the wall behind me, and his jaw tightens. He uses the clinical term-"visual intrusions"-as if naming it will contain the memory of the shattered storefront and the crimson that stained the white dust.

For years, he managed. He threw himself into his studies, left Pakistan for his doctorate in the United States, and built a successful practice. He met and married his wife, Aisha. He believed his clinical training had inoculated him, that he had the tools to process and file away the event. He saw it as a closed chapter, a defining but distant part of his history. He specialized in trauma, telling himself it was a way to make sense of what happened, to bring order to the chaos.

The facade began to crack about a year ago. A patient was describing a severe car accident, and as she spoke of the sound of twisting metal, Samir felt the floor drop out from under him. The air in his hermetically sealed office suddenly tasted of dust. He felt his heart hammer against his ribs, a wild bird trapped in a cage. He managed to get through the session, but something had broken loose.

Now, the past is no longer past. He has nightmares most nights, waking up drenched in sweat, his heart racing, the images from the cafe replaying in vivid detail. He finds himself constantly scanning his environment-restaurants, movie theaters, even his own waiting room-clocking the exits, assessing the people around him, a low hum of anxiety his constant companion. A car backfiring on the street sent him diving to the floor in his kitchen last month, leaving Aisha terrified and him awash in a profound, debilitating shame.

He feels like a fraud. How can he guide others through their darkness when he is so utterly lost in his own? The empathy he was once proud of now feels like a liability, a porous boundary that lets his patients' pain seep in and mingle with his. He describes a growing emotional numbness, a chasm widening between him and Aisha. She tells him he's a ghost in their home, present in body but absent in spirit. He knows she's right. He listens to her, nodding with the practiced air of a therapist, while feeling nothing but a vast, hollow emptiness. He is an expert on the map of trauma, but he is living in the territory, and he no longer knows which way to turn.
